files.README.md:
# Freelance Proposal Kit

Turn "can you send me a quote?" into a proposal the client can say yes to. This kit gives you a proposal template with a fully completed example, a simple way to offer three priced options, follow-up emails for every stage, a pre-send checklist and a tracker that shows which proposals win and why.

It is built for solo freelancers and small studios who write proposals for project work: design, writing, development, marketing, video, consulting and similar.

## What's inside

| File | Use it for |
|---|---|
| proposal-template.md | A one-to-three page proposal you fill in, followed by a completed example for a real-looking project. |
| pricing-options.md | How to turn one quote into three options (Essential, Standard, Complete), with a worked example and the maths behind it. |
| follow-up-emails.md | Seven ready-to-send emails: sending the proposal, three follow-ups, handling "it's too expensive", accepting, and closing the loop politely. |
| proposal-checklist.md | Twenty checks to run before you hit send, grouped by what goes wrong most often. |
| proposal-tracker.csv | One row per proposal: value, option chosen, outcome and the reason. Open it in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers. |

## Quick start (30 minutes, once)

1. Read the completed example at the end of **proposal-template.md**. It shows the tone and length to aim for.
2. Save the blank template as your own document. Fill in the parts that never change: your name, your process, your standard terms.
3. Read **pricing-options.md** and decide what your three options would be for your most common type of project.
4. Put your name and sign-off into the brackets in **follow-up-emails.md**.
5. Open **proposal-tracker.csv**, delete the three example rows and add your next proposal.

## How to use it for each new proposal (45-90 minutes)

1. Have a short discovery call or email exchange first. Never write a proposal for a project you have not discussed.
2. Copy your saved template and fill in the client's goal **in their words**, then your plan, options and timeline.
3. Price the three options using **pricing-options.md**.
4. Run **proposal-checklist.md**.
5. Send it with email 1 from **follow-up-emails.md**, and set reminders for the follow-ups.
6. Log it in **proposal-tracker.csv** the same day, and record the outcome when you hear back.

## Tips that make the biggest difference

- **Lead with their problem, not your bio.** The first thing the client reads should be their own goal, said back to them clearly.
- **Keep it short.** Most winning freelance proposals are one to three pages. Length rarely wins work; clarity does.
- **Give a decision date.** "This proposal is valid until [date]" gives both of you a natural point to follow up.
- **Make saying yes easy.** End with exactly what happens next: reply to accept, deposit invoice, kickoff date.
- **Track every result.** After ten proposals you will see your real win rate and which option people pick. That is how you raise prices with confidence.

## Notes

The templates are general business writing, not legal advice. If you work on large projects or in a regulated field, have your contract terms reviewed by a professional where you work. The example names, figures and companies in this kit are made up for illustration.

This kit pairs well with the Freelance Client Onboarding Kit (what to do after they say yes) and the Freelancer Get-Paid Kit (invoicing and payment reminders).

# Proposal template

Copy everything between the two lines into a document. Replace every [bracket]. Delete any section that doesn't apply. Aim for one to three pages.

A completed example follows the blank template.

---

**Prepared by:** [Your name], [Your business name]
**Date:** [Date]
**Valid until:** [Date, usually 14 days later]

# Completed example

The client, names and figures below are invented to show how a finished proposal reads.

---

# Proposal: Website refresh for Harbour Lane Physio

**Prepared for:** Dana Whitfield, Practice Manager, Harbour Lane Physio
**Prepared by:** Sam Rivera, Rivera Web Studio
**Date:** 4 November
**Valid until:** 18 November

## 1. Where you are now

Your site was built six years ago and is hard to update. Most new patients find you on their phones, but booking takes four taps and a phone call, and you told me the front desk spends "an hour a day answering the same five questions." You want more online bookings and fewer routine calls.

## 2. What success looks like

By the end of this project you will have:

- A mobile-friendly site that your team can update without help
- A booking button on every page that links straight to your existing booking system
- A clear FAQ and services section that answers the questions your front desk hears most

## 3. How I'll get you there

| Stage | What happens | What you'll get |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Discovery | 60-minute call with you and one front-desk staff member; review of your current site and analytics | One-page plan and site map |
| 2. Design | Layout for the home page and one service page | Two page designs to review |
| 3. Build | Full site built on an easy editor, content moved across | Working site on a private preview link |
| 4. Launch and training | Go live, check everything, 45-minute training session | Live site, recorded training, one-page guide |

## 4. Options and investment

| | Essential | Standard | Complete |
|---|---|---|---|
| Up to 6 pages built and content moved | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Booking button and mobile layout | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| FAQ page written from your top questions | - | Yes | Yes |
| Rewritten copy for services pages | - | Yes | Yes |
| Basic search setup (titles, descriptions, map listing check) | - | - | Yes |
| 30 days of post-launch fixes and edits | - | - | Yes |
| Rounds of revisions | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| Timeline | 4 weeks | 5 weeks | 6 weeks |
| **Price** | **$2,400** | **$3,600** | **$4,900** |

I recommend **Standard**: the FAQ and rewritten service pages are what will cut down the routine calls you mentioned.

## 5. Timeline (Standard)

- **11 November**: Kickoff call
- **18 November**: Plan and site map agreed
- **29 November**: Designs ready to review
- **10 December**: Preview site ready
- **16 December**: Launch and training

The timeline assumes feedback within 2 working days at each stage.

## 6. What's not included

- Changes to your booking system itself
- Photography (I can recommend a local photographer)
- Ongoing hosting fees, which are paid directly to the provider

## 7. What I need from you

- Login access to your current site and domain
- A list of the questions your front desk answers most often
- Dana as the main contact to approve each stage

## 8. Terms

- **Payment:** 50% deposit to book the start date, 50% on launch. Invoices are due within 14 days.
- **Revisions:** As listed above. Extra rounds are $250 each.
- **Changes in scope:** New requests are quoted in writing before work starts.
- **Ownership:** You own the site and its content once paid in full.
- **Cancellation:** The deposit covers work done to date and is non-refundable after the kickoff call.

## 9. Next steps

1. Reply to this email with the option you'd like.
2. I'll send the agreement and deposit invoice the same day.
3. Once the deposit is paid, your 11 November start is booked.

Sam Rivera
sam@example.com | 555-0142
files.pricing-options.md:
# Pricing with three options

One price gives the client one question: yes or no. Three options change the question to "which one?", and let clients who value more pay for more. This guide shows how to build them without guessing.

## The three options

| Option | Who it's for | How to build it |
|---|---|---|
| **Essential** | Tight budget, needs the core result | The smallest version that still solves the main problem. Never a broken or useless version. |
| **Standard** | Most clients. This is the one you recommend. | Everything they asked for on the call, done properly. |
| **Complete** | Wants it handled end to end | Standard plus the things that save them time or reduce risk: extra support, extra revisions, related tasks they would otherwise do themselves. |

## Step 1: Price the Standard option first

1. List every task in the project.
2. Estimate hours for each task. Be honest; most people underestimate.
3. Add a buffer of 15-25% for calls, emails, revisions and surprises.
4. Multiply by your hourly rate. If you don't know your rate, work it out first with a rate calculator, starting from the income you need.
5. Round to a clean number.

**Worked example (from the completed proposal):**

| Task | Hours |
|---|---|
| Discovery call and plan | 4 |
| Two page designs | 8 |
| Build 6 pages and move content | 16 |
| FAQ page | 3 |
| Rewrite service pages | 5 |
| Launch, checks and training | 4 |
| **Subtotal** | **40** |
| Buffer 20% | 8 |
| **Total** | **48 hours** |

48 hours x $75 per hour = $3,600. Standard price: **$3,600**.

## Step 2: Build Essential by removing, not discounting

Take tasks out until you reach the core result. Price what remains the same way.

In the example, removing the FAQ page and rewritten copy (8 hours plus buffer, about 10 hours) and one revision round gives roughly 32 hours, or **$2,400**.

Never offer the same work for less money. If the client can get Standard at the Essential price by asking, your prices stop meaning anything.

## Step 3: Build Complete by adding value, not just hours

Add things that matter to this client: support after launch, a training session, extra revisions, a related task on their to-do list. Price the extra hours, then add a premium of 10-20% for the extra responsibility and priority.

In the example: search setup (4 hours) plus 30 days of fixes (estimated 8 hours) plus one more revision round (4 hours) is 16 hours, or $1,200. Add a 10% premium on those extras ($120) and the total is $4,920, rounded to **$4,900**.

## Step 4: Check the spread

A useful rule of thumb: Essential is about 60-70% of Standard, and Complete is about 130-150% of Standard. If the gap is much smaller, the options feel the same. If it is much bigger, Complete looks out of reach.

| | Essential | Standard | Complete |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example | $2,400 | $3,600 | $4,900 |
| Share of Standard | 67% | 100% | 136% |

## Step 5: Recommend one

Always say which option you recommend and give one reason tied to the client's goal. Most clients will choose it, and the others are there for the ones who need them.

## When not to use three options

- Very small jobs (under a few hours). Give one clear price.
- Fixed-scope work the client has fully specified. Offer one price and, at most, one optional add-on.
- Retainers. Offer hour or deliverable bundles instead, for example 10, 20 or 30 hours a month.

## Handling "can you do it cheaper?"

Point back to the options rather than cutting the price: "If budget is the main concern, Essential gets you [core result] for [$]. We could add the FAQ page later as a separate small project." This keeps your rate intact and keeps the conversation open.

## Your own options worksheet

Copy this for your most common type of project:

| | Essential | Standard | Complete |
|---|---|---|---|
| Included tasks | | | |
| Hours (with buffer) | | | |
| Revisions | | | |
| Timeline | | | |
| Price | | | |
| Share of Standard | | 100% | |
files.follow-up-emails.md:
# Proposal emails

Seven emails for every stage after the discovery call. Replace the [brackets]. Keep them short; most clients read on a phone.

Suggested timing:

| Email | When to send |
|---|---|
| 1. Sending the proposal | Within 2 working days of the discovery call |
| 2. First follow-up | 3 working days after sending, if no reply |
| 3. Second follow-up | 7 working days after sending |
| 4. Final follow-up | On or just before the "valid until" date |
| 5. "It's too expensive" | When they push back on price |
| 6. Accepted | Same day they say yes |
| 7. Declined | Same day they say no |

---

## 1. Sending the proposal

**Subject:** Proposal for [project name]

Hi [Name],

Thanks again for the call on [day]. As promised, here's my proposal for [project name].

In short: [one sentence on the outcome they want]. I've included three options, and I recommend **[option]** because [reason tied to their goal].

The proposal is valid until [date]. If it looks right, just reply with the option you'd like and I'll send the agreement and deposit invoice the same day.

Happy to jump on a quick call if anything needs talking through.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 2. First follow-up

**Subject:** Re: Proposal for [project name]

Hi [Name],

Just checking the proposal arrived safely and made sense. Do you have any questions I can answer, or anything you'd like me to adjust?

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 3. Second follow-up

**Subject:** Re: Proposal for [project name]

Hi [Name],

I know these decisions often involve other people, so no rush. If it helps, I can send a short summary you could forward to [their boss / partner / the team].

I'm currently booking projects to start from [date], so let me know if you'd like me to hold that slot for you.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 4. Final follow-up

**Subject:** Re: Proposal for [project name]

Hi [Name],

The proposal I sent is valid until [date], so I wanted to check in one last time before then.

If the timing isn't right, that's completely fine. Just let me know and I'll close the file for now. If things change later, I'd be happy to put together an updated proposal.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 5. When they say it's too expensive

**Subject:** Re: Proposal for [project name]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for being upfront, that's helpful. A couple of ways we could make this work:

- **Essential** covers [core result] for [$]. We could add [removed item] later as a separate small project.
- We could split the payments into [three] instalments across the project.
- We could reduce the scope to [smaller version] for [$].

Which of these is closest to what you need?

Best,
[Your name]

(Offer smaller scope or different payment timing. Avoid simply cutting the price for the same work.)

---

## 6. When they accept

**Subject:** Great, let's get started on [project name]

Hi [Name],

Wonderful, thank you for choosing [option]. Here's what happens next:

1. Attached is the agreement. Please sign and return it.
2. The [50]% deposit invoice is attached, due by [date].
3. Once both are in, I'll confirm our kickoff call on [date].

Looking forward to working together.

Best,
[Your name]

---

## 7. When they decline

**Subject:** Re: Proposal for [project name]

Hi [Name],

Thanks for letting me know, and for considering me. If you don't mind sharing, was there one main reason it wasn't the right fit? It helps me improve, and there's no wrong answer.

I hope the project goes well, and please keep me in mind if anything comes up in future.

Best,
[Your name]

(Log their reason in proposal-tracker.csv. Patterns in these answers are some of the most useful information you will get.)
files.proposal-checklist.md:
# Pre-send proposal checklist

Run through this before every proposal. It takes five minutes and catches the mistakes that lose work or cause arguments later.

## The client's problem

- [ ] The first section describes their situation in their own words, not your services.
- [ ] The outcomes are things they can see or measure, not activities ("more online bookings", not "design work").
- [ ] Their name and company are spelled correctly everywhere, including the file name.
- [ ] No leftover text from another client's proposal. Search the document for the last client's name.

## Scope

- [ ] Every deliverable is listed, with how many (pages, videos, drafts, hours).
- [ ] The number of revision rounds is stated for each option.
- [ ] "What's not included" lists at least two things they might assume are included.
- [ ] "What I need from you" lists access, content and who approves the work.

## Price

- [ ] Each option has one clear total, not a range.
- [ ] You have said which option you recommend and why.
- [ ] Essential removes work; it does not just discount Standard.
- [ ] The price includes a buffer for calls, revisions and surprises.
- [ ] Tax or currency is stated if it could cause confusion.

## Timeline and terms

- [ ] Dates are realistic, with your other projects in mind.
- [ ] The timeline says what happens if feedback is late.
- [ ] Deposit, payment due dates and what happens on cancellation are stated.
- [ ] Who owns the work, and from when, is stated.
- [ ] The "valid until" date is filled in.

## Making it easy to say yes

- [ ] Next steps are numbered and specific (reply, agreement, deposit, start date).
- [ ] It's one to three pages, or there's a very good reason it's longer.
- [ ] Saved as a PDF (or shared link) with a clear name: ClientName-Proposal-Date.
- [ ] Logged in proposal-tracker.csv with follow-up dates set in your calendar.
